en: The Water Repentance Ritual (Cibei Shuichan Fa), Scroll One.
All Buddhas, out of compassion for sentient beings, have expounded the general rules for the water repentance ritual site (*maṇḍala*). The Buddha said:
"The defilements of sentient beings are heavy. Who among them is without sin? Who is without transgression? Ordinary people act with folly."
Enveloped by the darkness of ignorance,
they associate with evil friends, their minds distracted by afflictions;
being ignorant by nature, they act willfully and rely on their own conceit.
They do not believe in the Buddhas of the ten directions;
they do not believe in the Honored Dharma or the Noble Sangha;
they are unfilial toward their parents and their six kinds of relatives and kin.
In the prime of their youth, they were dissolute and self-conceited;
they craved all manner of wealth and treasures,
and they craved all manner of song and music.
They crave all forms of female beauty;
their minds give rise to longing and afflictions,
and they associate with those who are unholy and familiarize themselves with evil friends.
They do not know how to repent;
they may kill all sentient beings or drink alcohol until they are intoxicated and deluded.
Lacking wisdom in my heart,
today I lay bare my sincerity and repent one by one for all past transgressions and the various evils committed in the present.
Today, with sincere resolve, we repent for all [our transgressions].
We dare not commit again those sins we have yet to commit.
Disciple [Name] and the others today offer this with a devoted heart.
I take refuge in all Buddhas throughout the ten directions and the entirety of the realm of empty space;
in all great Bodhisattvas, Pratyekabuddhas, and Arhats of the four fruits and four stages of realization;
and in the Brahma Kings and Śakras.
May all the holy assemblies of the eight classes of devas and nāgas deign to bear witness. Homage to Vairocana Buddha; homage to our original teacher Śākyamuni Buddha;

homage to Amitābha Buddha; homage to Maitreya Buddha; homage to Nāgottamarāja Buddha; homage to Nāgeśvararāja Buddha; homage to Ratnasaṃbhava Buddha; homage to Bodhimaṇḍitavikrīḍitābhijña Buddha; homage to Kāśyapadhvaja Buddha; homage to Siṃhanāda Buddha; homage to Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva; homage to Samantabhadra Bodhisattva; homage to Mahāsthāmaprāpta Bodhisattva; homage to Kṣitigarbha Bodhisattva; homage to Mahāvyūha Bodhisattva; homage to Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva. Having paid homage to all the Buddhas, [I now...]
Next, one performs repentance.
Now, those who wish to perform prostrations and repentance must first show reverence to the Triple Gem; the reason for this is as follows:
The Three Jewels are the true friends and fields of merit for all sentient beings.
If one can take refuge in them, immeasurable sins will be extinguished and immeasurable blessings will increase.
It enables the practitioner to leave behind the suffering of birth and death and attain the bliss of liberation.

For this reason, disciples such as [Name], we take refuge in all Buddhas throughout the ten directions and the entirety of space; we take refuge in all Honored Dharmas throughout the ten directions and the entirety of space; and we take refuge in all Noble Sanghas throughout the ten directions and the entirety of space. The reason the disciples repent today is...
To speak truthfully, from time immemorial while remaining on the stage of an ordinary person,
regardless of whether one is noble or lowly, offenses have been immeasurable;
these offenses may arise due to the three karmas of body, speech, and mind.
Either faults arise from the six sense faculties,
or they stem from one's own internal improper reflection,
or they originate through attachment to external objects.
In this way, it extends even to the ten evil deeds,
which increase the eighty-four thousand gates of worldly affliction; yet,
although the characteristics of these transgressions are immeasurable, [they are all subsumed within them].
Broadly speaking, there are no more than three types of awakening:
first, afflictions; second, karma.
The third is the retribution itself.
These three types of phenomena can obstruct the Noble Path as well as the excellent and sublime matters of humans and devas;
therefore, they are designated as the "three obstructions" in the sūtras.
For this reason, the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas teach the performance of skillful means through repentance in order to eliminate these three obstacles.
Then the six sense organs, the ten unwholesome actions,
and even the eighty-four thousand gates of affliction will all become completely pure.
For this reason, we, the disciples such as [Name], etc., [prostrate ourselves].
Today, I shall employ this superior and sublime resolve to repent of the three obstructions.
Those who wish to extinguish the three obstructions should employ what kind of mind?
One may cause these hindrances to be extinguished.
First, one should give rise to seven kinds of mental states as a preliminary means;
only then can these hindrances be eliminated.
What are the seven?
First is shame and remorse; second is fear.
Third is weary detachment;
fourth is the arousal of the bodhicitta;
fifth is equanimity toward enemies and kin.
Sixth, mindfulness of repaying the Buddha’s kindness;
seventh, contemplating the emptiness of the nature of offenses.
First, regarding shame and remorse:
I reflect upon myself:
I and Śākyamuni Tathāgata were once both ordinary beings.
Yet since the World-Honored One attained the Way,
an incalculable number of kalpas as vast as the sands of the Ganges has already passed,
and we have remained here together, indulging in worldly attachments.
Being stained by the six sense objects, one revolves through birth and death with no end in sight;
this is truly something in the world that should cause shame, remorse, embarrassment, and disgrace.
As for the second terror:
Since the physical, verbal, and mental actions of an ordinary person are constantly associated with transgressions,
by reason of these causes and conditions, after the end of life,
they ought to fall into the hells, the animal realm, or the realm of hungry ghosts to undergo immeasurable suffering.
Thus, this is truly something to be marveled at, to be terrified by, to be fearful of, and to be alarmed by.
Third, as for wearying detachment:
one constantly contemplates the midst of birth and death.
Only impermanence, suffering, emptiness, and non-self;
impure and illusory like bubbles upon the water,
arising and ceasing with great speed.
Wandering and revolving like a chariot wheel,
one is tormented by the eight sufferings of birth, old age, sickness,
and death, with no moment of respite.
All of you together should simply observe your own bodies from head to foot;
within them, there are nothing but thirty-six things.

Hair, body hair, nails, teeth, eye-secretions, tears, nasal mucus, saliva, filth, sweat, the two excretions, skin, flesh, blood, tendons, vessels, bone marrow, fat, grease, brain membrane, spleen, kidneys, heart, lungs, liver, gallbladder, intestines, stomach, and the two internal organs—the raw and the cooked—along with red and white phlegm and mucus.
Thus, these nine orifices flow constantly;
therefore, the Sūtra says:
"This body is a collection of manifold sufferings."
All things are impure.
What wise person would take pleasure in this body?
Since birth and death involve such various evil phenomena as these, [how could one find delight in them?]
It is truly something to be deeply weary of and loathe.
Regarding the fourth [type], those who have resolved to attain bodhicitta,
the Sūtra says:
One should take delight in the Buddha-body.
The Buddha-body is the Dharma-body; it is born from immeasurable merit and wisdom.
It arises from the six pāramitās;
it arises from loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity;
it arises from the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment.
The body of a Tathāgata is born from such various merits and wisdom.
Those who wish to attain this body should resolve upon bodhicitta and seek all-encompassing knowledge (sarvākārajñatā).
The fruit of omniscience (*sarvajñatā*) is eternal, blissful, self, and pure;
it purifies buddha-fields, brings sentient beings to maturity,
and involves no stinginess regarding one's body, life, or wealth.
Fifth, regarding equanimity toward enemies and kin:
one gives rise to a mind of loving-kindness and compassion toward all sentient beings, free from the distinction between "self" and "other."
Why is this so? If one perceives the enemy as distinct from the relative, that is conceptual discrimination (*vikalpa*).
Because of such discrimination, various attachments to signs (*nimitta*) arise.
Through the causal conditions of mutual attachment, various afflictions arise.
Through the causal conditions of afflictions, various evil karmas are created.
Due to the causal conditions of evil karma, one obtains bitter fruits.
Sixth, regarding the mindfulness of repaying the Buddha’s kindness:
throughout immeasurable kalpas in the past, the Tathāgata sacrificed his head,
eyes, marrow, brain, limbs, joints, hands, and feet.
For our sake, he practiced various ascetic austerities, relinquishing his kingdom, city, wife, children, elephants, horses, and the seven treasures;
this kindness and virtue are truly difficult to repay.
Therefore, the Sūtra says:
"Even if one were to carry [the Buddha's teachings] upon the crown of one's head or on both shoulders for kalpas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, one could never repay [them]."
Those of us who wish to repay such kindness as this should,
in this world, exert ourselves with courageous diligence;
we shall endure toil and hardship, not begrudging our own bodies or lives.
To establish the Triple Gem, propagate the Mahāyāna, and extensively transform sentient beings so that they may together enter perfect enlightenment.
Seventh, regarding the contemplation of the emptiness of the nature of offenses: offenses have no self-nature; they arise from causes and conditions.
They exist through inversion;
since they arise from causes and conditions,
they can likewise cease through causes and conditions.
That which arises from causes and conditions does so by associating with evil friends and acting without cause.
That which ceases from causes and conditions likewise [does so].
This is precisely what is meant by washing the mind and repenting today.
Therefore, the Sūtra says:
"The nature of this transgression does not reside within."
It does not exist externally,
nor does it exist in between; therefore,
one knows that this transgression is fundamentally empty.
Having generated these seven kinds of mind, one visualizes the Buddhas and holy sages of the ten directions, joining the palms with hands raised in reverence,
laying bare one's heart with utmost sincerity, and reforming through shame and remorse.
It thoroughly traverses the heart and liver and cleanses the intestines and stomach.
Through such repentance, what transgression would not be extinguished,
and what merit would not be generated?
If it were otherwise,
and one were to remain lax and negligent, allowing the mind to wander and become restless,
it would merely be a waste of physical effort; what benefit would there be in such affairs?
Furthermore, human life is impermanent,
comparable to a flickering candle;
if one breath does not return, it is as good as being reduced to dust and earth.
The retributions of suffering in the three evil realms must be experienced by one’s own body;
they cannot be escaped through the mediation of money, wealth, or treasures.
In the profound and dark abyss, there is no hope for pardon or amnesty.
I alone am beset by this suffering with no one to take it upon themselves;
do not say that such transgressions did not exist within my present life,
for that is why I have been unable to offer earnest prayers and repentance.
The sutra states:
"For ordinary persons, every lifting of a foot and every movement of a step is nothing but sin;
furthermore, throughout their past lives, they have fully accomplished immeasurable evil karma."
They pursue the practitioner like a shadow following a form;
if one does not repent, their transgressions will deepen daily.
Thus, one should know that the Buddha does not permit the concealment of flaws.
Confessing prior transgressions is what the Honored One of Pure Name (Vimalakīrti) esteemed;
thus, our long immersion in the sea of suffering is truly due to concealment and suppression.
Therefore, I, disciple [Name], today openly confess and repent, no longer concealing anything.
What are called the three obstacles are:
first, afflictions; second, karma;
and third, retribution.
These three types of phenomena depend upon one another:
because of afflictions, various evil karmas arise;
and due to the conditions of those evil karmas, bitter fruits are obtained.
Therefore, this disciple [Name], today with a sincere heart, repents.
First, one should repent of the obstacle of afflictions (*kleśāvaraṇa*).
These afflictions all arise from the mind.
Why is this? Because when mental karma arises,
the body and speech follow along and move accordingly.
There are three types of mental karma:
first, stinginess and greed;
second, anger and hatred.
Third is the darkness of delusion.
Because of this darkness of delusion, one gives rise to various false views and commits various unwholesome deeds.
Therefore, the Sūtra says:
The karma of greed, hatred, and delusion causes sentient beings to fall into the realms of hell, hungry ghosts, and animals, where they undergo suffering.
If they are born among humans, they will encounter poverty, destitution, and exposure, and will be fierce, violent, stubborn, and dull-witted.
These are the retributions for the afflictions of ignorance and delusion.
Since the karma of the mind has such evil fruits, we,
[Name] and others, today take refuge in all Buddhas with a sincere heart.
I seek your compassion and repent.
Indeed, these afflictions have been rebuked in various ways by all Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, and noble ones who have entered into the truth.
These afflictions are also called enemies.
Why? Because they sever the life-root of wisdom in sentient beings.
These afflictions are also called "thieves," for they are able to plunder the various wholesome dharmas of sentient beings. They are also called "floods."
Because they can carry sentient beings away into the great ocean of suffering of birth and death,
these afflictions are also called "floods.
Because they can bind sentient beings within the prison of birth and death so that they cannot escape, they are also called "chains."
Thus, the six realms are interconnected and the four modes of birth are never-ending;
evil karma is inexhaustible and the fruits of suffering do not cease.
One should know that all of this is the fault and affliction of the defilements.
Therefore, today we mobilize this superior mind of goodness to seek compassion and repent.
We, [Name] and others, from beginningless time until this very day, have been receiving retribution while transmigrating through the six realms of existence, including the human and celestial realms.
Possessing this mind-consciousness, one constantly harbors ignorance and delusion, which fill the breast;
or, due to the three roots of poison, one commits all manner of transgressions;
or, due to the three outflows, one commits all manner of transgressions.
Either they commit all manner of transgressions due to the three types of suffering;
or they commit all manner of transgressions conditioned by the three inversions;
or they commit all manner of transgressions out of craving for the three realms of existence.
Such offenses as these are immeasurable and boundless;
they have disturbed and troubled all beings within the six realms and four modes of birth.
Today, with shame and remorse, I confess them all.
Furthermore, such-and-such individuals, from beginningless time until this very day,
have committed all manner of transgressions due to the four stations of consciousness,
or have committed all manner of transgressions due to the four floods.
Or one may commit all manner of transgressions due to the four graspings;
or due to the four attachments; or due to the four conditions.
Or one may commit all manner of transgressions due to the four great elements;
or one may commit all manner of transgressions due to the four fetters;
or one may commit all manner of transgressions due to the four cravings.
Or, due to the four modes of birth, they commit all manner of transgressions.
Such offenses as these are immeasurable and boundless,
afflicting and disturbing all sentient beings throughout the six realms.
Today, with shame and remorse, we confess all of these. Furthermore,
from beginningless time until this day, we, such-and-such individuals and others, have committed every kind of transgression,
whether due to the afflictions of the five stages of dwelling or otherwise.
Or one may commit all manner of offenses due to the five hindrances;
or one may commit all manner of offenses due to the five types of stinginess;
or one may commit all manner of offenses due to the five views.
Or, one may commit all manner of transgressions through the five minds.
Thus, these afflictions are immeasurable and boundless,
tormenting and disorienting all sentient beings throughout the six realms.
Today we openly disclose and repent of them all.
Furthermore, from time immemorial until this day, we, such-and-such individuals,
have committed every kind of transgression through the six sense faculties.
Or one may commit all manner of offenses due to the six consciousnesses;
or one may commit all manner of offenses due to the six perceptions;
or one may commit all manner of offenses due to the six feelings.
Or one may commit all manner of offenses due to the six modes of conduct;
or one may commit all manner of offenses due to the six cravings;
or one may commit all manner of offenses due to the six doubts.
Such afflictions as these are immeasurable and boundless,
tormenting all sentient beings throughout the six realms.
Today, with shame and remorse, I reveal them all and repent for every one.
Furthermore, such-and-such persons, from beginningless time until this day,
have committed all manner of transgressions due to the seven outflows (*āsrava*),
or have committed all manner of transgressions due to the seven latent tendencies (*anuśaya*).
Or one may commit all manner of transgressions due to the eight inversions;
or one may commit all manner of transgressions due to the eight impurities;
or one may commit all manner of transgressions due to the eight sufferings.
Such afflictions as these are immeasurable and boundless,
tormenting all sentient beings throughout the six realms.
Today, I openly disclose them and repent for them all.
Furthermore, such-and-such persons as myself, from beginningless time until this day,
have committed all manner of transgressions due to the nine causes of resentment.
Or one may commit all manner of transgressions due to the nine fetters;
or one may commit all manner of transgressions due to the nine conditions;
or one may commit all manner of transgressions due to the ten afflictions.
Or one may commit all manner of offenses due to the ten fetters (*paryavasthāna*);
or due to the eleven pervasive proclivities (*anuśaya*);
or due to the twelve sense bases (*āyatana*).
Or one may commit all manner of transgressions due to the sixteen types of false views;
or due to the eighteen elements (dhātus);
or due to the twenty-five notions of self (ātman).
Or, one may commit all manner of transgressions due to the sixty-two views;
or, due to those views,
one reflects upon the ninety-eight underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) and the one hundred and eight afflictions (*kleśa*).
Day and night, burning fiercely, they open the gates of all outflows,
commit every kind of transgression,
and harass the noble ones and sages.
Together with the four modes of birth,
they pervade the three realms and extend throughout the six paths of existence.
There is no place to escape.
Today I pray to the Buddhas of the ten directions, the Honored Dharma, and the Assembly of Sages;
with shame and remorse, I confess and repent for all my transgressions.
May we, such-and-such persons, by virtue of the merit generated through this confession of the three poisons and all afflictions,
in birth after birth and throughout every lifetime...
May the three types of wisdom be clarified and the three types of supernormal knowledge be made radiant; may the three sufferings be extinguished and the three vows be fulfilled.
By virtue of this repentance, may these aspirations be realized.
Through the merits produced by all afflictions such as the four consciousnesses,
and by extensively cultivating the four immeasurable minds (*catur-apramāṇa*) and establishing the karma of the four reliances (*catuḥ-pratisaraṇa*) throughout successive lifetimes,
one extinguishes the four evil destinies and attains the four fearlessnesses (*catur-vaiśāradya*).
By virtue of this repentance,
may the merit produced from the five hindrances and all other afflictions enable one to cross over the five paths, erect the five faculties,
purify the five eyes, and accomplish the five aggregates.
I vow that by virtue of the merit arising from these confessions and the various afflictions such as the six types of sensation,
may I be fully endowed with the six supernormal powers in birth after birth throughout all lifetimes.
May I fulfill the karma of the six perfections and remain undeluded by the six sense objects,
constantly practicing the six subtle conducts. Furthermore,

I vow that by virtue of the merit produced from this repentance of all afflictions— the seven outflows, eight impurities, nine fetters, ten entanglements, and so forth— [may these benefits be attained].
In birth after birth, may they sit upon the seven flowers of purity,
bathe in the waters of the eight liberations,
and be endowed with the nine knowledges of abandonment.

May the merit produced by this elevenfold repentance— which accomplishes the practices of the ten stages (daśabhūmi)— as well as that produced regarding the twelve bases (āyatana) and eighteen elements (dhātu), and all other afflictions, [be dedicated for the benefit of all beings].
May the eleven emptinesses enable one to understand their constant application and allow the mind to dwell in sovereign freedom.
He is able to turn the Dharma wheel of twelve aspects;
he is fully endowed with the eighteen unique qualities;
and all his immeasurable merits are perfectly complete.

Having made this vow, one takes refuge and pays homage to all Buddhas: Namo Vairocana Buddha. Namo Śākyamuni Buddha, our Original Teacher. Namo Amitābha Buddha. Namo Maitreya Buddha. Namo Nāgottamarāja Buddha. Namo Nāgeśvararāja Buddha. Namo Ratnasaṃbhava Buddha. Namo Bodhimaṇḍitavikrīḍitaśrīrāja Buddha. Namo Kāśyapadhvaja Buddha. Namo Siṃhanāda Buddha. Namo Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva. Namo Samantabhadra Bodhisattva. Namo Mahāsthāmaprāpta Bodhisattva. Namo Kṣitigarbha Bodhisattva. Namo Mahāvyūha Bodhisattva. Namo Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva. Having paid homage to all the Buddhas, [one continues].
Next, perform repentance.
Now, as for what is called repentance,
it fundamentally consists of reforming the past and cultivating the future.
To extinguish evil and promote good:
who among those dwelling in this world can be without transgression?
Even a student on the path, when losing mindfulness, still gives rise to afflictions.
Even Arhats have residual habits that stir up physical and verbal karma;
how much more so, then, could ordinary people be without transgression?
However, the wise, through their prior awakening, are able to reform and repent.
The foolish conceal their faults, causing them to spread like creeping vines;
thus, through long nights of habitual practice, there is no prospect of awakening.
If one can feel shame and remorse, revealing and repenting for them, [the situation may be remedied].
Not only does this extinguish transgressions,
but it also increases immeasurable merit and establishes the sublime fruit of the Tathāgata’s nirvāṇa.
If one wishes to practice this dharma,
one should first externally solemnize one's physical demeanor while gazing upon and revering the sacred image;
internally, one should give rise to a spirit of respect and focus the mind on the object of contemplation.
With earnest and sincere prayer, one should give rise to two kinds of thoughts. What are these two?
First, one reflects upon oneself.
This physical life of mine is difficult to preserve forever;
were it to perish in a single day, I would not know when this body could ever be restored.
Furthermore, if I do not encounter the Buddhas, sages, and holy ones...
First, one suddenly encounters evil friends who commit various sinful karmas,
and one will consequently fall into deep pits and perilous realms;
second, one reflects within oneself.
Although I have encountered the True Dharma of the Tathāgata in this life,
I have not succeeded to the noble lineage of the Buddha-dharma; rather,
I have dwelt in the wholesome dharmas of purifying body, speech, and mind.
Now we have privately committed evil deeds and yet conceal them,
claiming that others do not know of them;
thinking that they do not see us, we hide our wickedness within our hearts, remaining arrogant and shameless.
This is truly the height of delusion and folly in the world.
Right now, there are the Buddhas of the ten directions, the great Bodhisattvas, and the devas and immortals;
how could they not have seen with their pure divine eyes the evil deeds we have committed?
Furthermore, the spirits of both the hidden and the manifest record one’s sins and merits with not even a hair’s breadth of error.
Now, regarding those who commit transgressions:
After their lives have ended,
the ox-headed jailers record their spirits and bring them before King Yama.
To investigate and determine right from wrong— at that very moment—
all adversaries will come forward to provide testimony.
Each said: "Previously you slaughtered my body, roasting, boiling, steaming, and grilling it;
or else you previously plundered all my wealth and treasures."
Separated from my retinue,
today I have finally found an opportunity against you;
at this moment, you stand before me as living witness.
How could one dare to conceal it?
One should only willingly accept and bear one's own share of past calamities,
as clearly explained in the sutras.
In the hells, no one is punished unjustly.
If, during one's ordinary life, one has committed various transgressions but has forgotten them in one's own mind,
then at the time of death, at the very place where those evils were committed—
All their various forms appeared before them,
and each said,
"In the past, you committed such-and-such a transgression against me."
How can one now hope to evade this?
At that time, there is no place for those who have committed sins to hide.
Thereupon, King Yama gnashes his teeth in reproach and consigns them to hell.
Having passed through immeasurable kalpas, there has been no way to seek liberation from this.
This matter is not far off and does not concern others;
it is precisely my own body that creates its own karma and must experience its own retribution.
Although father and son share the utmost intimacy,
when the ultimate moment arrives, there is no one who can take one's place;
we have all together obtained this human body.
The body is free from all ailments; each of you must exert yourselves and compete with your own lives.
When the great terror arrives, it will be too late for regret.
Therefore, with a sincere heart, we seek compassion and repent:
We, [Name] and others, from beginningless time until this day,
have accumulated ignorance that obscures the eyes and mind.
Following the nature of secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*), they commit offenses across the three periods of time;
or, through indulgence in defiled attachment, they give rise to the affliction of craving (*rāga*);
or, through hatred, anger, and malice, they harbor the affliction of resentment (*pratigha*).
There are the afflictions of mental confusion and delusion that lead to a lack of clarity;
the afflictions of self-conceit, arrogance, and haughtiness;
and the afflictions of doubt regarding the right path and indecisiveness.
The affliction of wrong views that deny cause and effect;
the affliction of failing to recognize dependent designation and clinging to a self;
and the affliction of being deluded regarding the three periods of time and adhering to the extremes of nihilism or eternalism.
Associating with evil dharmas gives rise to the affliction of dogmatic attachment to views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*).

Following the instructions of heterodox teachers leads to the affliction of dogmatic attachment to precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*). This extends to all such afflictions arising from the fourfold false conceptualizations.
Today, with utmost sincerity, I repent for all of this.
Furthermore, from time immemorial until this very day,
I have guarded and clung to possessions, giving rise to the affliction of stinginess.
The affliction of failing to restrain the six sense faculties and being extravagant;
the affliction of having a corrupt mind and conduct and lacking forbearance;
the affliction of indolence, laxity, and lack of diligence.
The affliction of doubt, agitation, applied thought, and sustained reflection;
the affliction of confusion and ignorance when encountering sensory objects;
and the affliction of "self" and "other" arising from the eight worldly winds.
The affliction of sycophancy and flattery, which lacks a straightforward mind;
the affliction of being wild and stubborn, difficult to approach, and lacking harmony;
and the affliction of being easily angered and difficult to please, harboring much resentment.
The affliction of jealousy, which strikes and wounds with extreme perversity;
the affliction of ferocity and violence, which is cruel and poisonous;
and the affliction of turning one's back on the Noble Truths while clinging to signs.
The afflictions that give rise to inversions regarding suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path;
the afflictions that follow along with the cycle of birth and death through the twelve links of dependent origination;
and even the *asaṃkhyeya* sands of afflictions within the ground of beginningless ignorance.
The afflictions arising from the four abodes give rise to the fruits of suffering within the triple world;
they are immeasurable and boundless,
vexing and disturbing the worthy and sages across the six destinies and four modes of birth.
Today, we openly confess before the Buddhas of the ten directions, the Honored Dharma, and the Assembly of Sages; may all be fully repented.
We pray that [Name] and others, by virtue of this confession, shall be purified of the greed, hatred, and delusion arising from the mental faculty.
All the merits arising from the afflictions serve,
in life after life, to break the banner of pride, exhaust the waters of craving and desire,
extinguish the fire of hatred, and shatter the darkness of ignorance.
They uproot the very root of doubt and tear asunder the net of all views;
they deeply realize that the three realms are like a prison and the four great elements are like venomous snakes.
The five aggregates are like vengeful bandits;
the six sense bases are an empty village where craving feigns intimacy.
One should cultivate the Eightfold Noble Path to sever the source of ignorance.
They are rightly directed toward nirvana, never ceasing and never resting.
The thirty-seven factors of enlightenment continue in succession from mind to mind,
and the ten perfections are constantly manifested before them.
Having completed the repentance, one should with a sincere heart take refuge in and pay homage to the eternally abiding Triple Gem.

All Buddhas, out of compassion for sentient beings, have taught the general dharmas of the Water Repentance Ritual Site.
Now, we take refuge in all Buddhas.

Homage to Vairocana Buddha. Homage to our Original Teacher Śākyamuni Buddha. Homage to Amitābha Buddha. Homage to Maitreya Buddha. Homage to Nāgottamarāja Buddha. Homage to Nāgeśvararāja Buddha. Homage to Ratnaśrī Buddha. Homage to Bodhimaṇḍa-vyūheśvararāja Buddha. Homage to Kāṣāyadhvaja Buddha. Homage to Siṃhanāda Buddha. Homage to Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva. Homage to Samantabhadra Bodhisattva. Homage to Mahāsthāmaprāpta Bodhisattva. Homage to Kṣitigarbha Bodhisattva. Homage to Mahāvyūha Bodhisattva. Homage to Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva. Having paid homage to all the Buddhas, [one should proceed].
Next, we further repent: we,
[Name] and others, together with one another,
now have our bodies and minds in a state of tranquility.
Free from flattery and free from obstruction,
this is precisely the time for generating the wholesome and extinguishing the unwholesome.
Furthermore, one should each give rise to four kinds of contemplative practices.
One considers these as preliminary practices for the eradication of offenses. What are the four?
First, contemplating causes and conditions.
Second, contemplating the karmic retribution;
third, contemplating one's own body;
fourth, contemplating the body of the Tathāgata.
First, regarding the contemplation of causes and conditions:
one knows that this transgression of mine arose by relying on ignorance and unwholesome reflection;
lacking the power of right observation, I failed to recognize its fault.
They distance themselves from virtuous friends— the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas—
and follow the path of Māra along treacherous and deviant ways;
like a fish swallowing a hook, they remain unaware of the danger.
Like a silkworm making a cocoon to entangle and bind itself,
or like a moth rushing into a flame to burn and rot itself,
by these causes and conditions it cannot emerge on its own.
Second, regarding the contemplation of karmic retribution:
all evil and unwholesome deeds result in the inexhaustible fruits of suffering as one transmigrates through the three periods of time.
They are submerged in the vast ocean of the great night of boundlessness,
devoured by the rākṣasas of the afflictions;
their future cycle of birth and death is dark and shoreless.
Even if one were to obtain as karmic retribution the status of a Wheel-Turning Sage King (cakravartin) ruling over the four continents,
possessing sovereign power to fly through the air and being endowed with the seven treasures,
one would still not escape the miserable realms after the end of life, nor the retributions of the four formless attainments (ārūpya-samāpatti).
Even those who were most honored in the three realms, when their merit is exhausted, become worms on the neck of an ox;
how much more so for others who possess no merit and yet remain indolent,
failing to diligently practice repentance?
This is also like the difficulty of seeking deliverance while clutching a stone and sinking into a deep abyss.
Third, one contemplates one's own person:
although one possesses the true cause, the nature of numinous awareness, it remains obscured.
Yet it is shrouded by the dense forest of the darkness of afflictions;
lacking the power of the cause of realization, it cannot be made manifest.
I shall now arouse a superior resolve to shatter the heavy obstructions of ignorance and perversion.
It severs the causes of the false suffering of birth and death,
manifests the Tathāgata’s great, luminous wisdom,
and establishes the sublime fruit of unsurpassed nirvāṇa.
The fourth contemplation is that of the Tathāgata’s body:
unconditioned, quiescent, and illuminating; transcending the four propositions and severing the hundred negations;
replete with all virtues, profound and eternally abiding.
Although he employs skillful means to enter parinirvāṇa,
his compassionate rescue and reception of beings is never for a moment abandoned.
To give rise to such a mind may be called an excellent ford for extinguishing transgressions and an essential practice for removing hindrances.
Therefore, with sincere resolve, we seek compassion and repent.
From beginningless time until this day, we have nurtured our afflictions,
which have grown ever deeper, ever thicker, ever more abundant, and ever more luxuriant.
It covers the eye of wisdom so that nothing may be seen;
it cuts off all wholesome roots so that they cannot continue;
and it gives rise to obstacles so that one cannot see the Buddha.
Not hearing the True Dharma,
not encountering the noble Sangha,
and giving rise to afflictions that create obstacles, they fail to see all past and future wholesome and unwholesome karmic actions.
The afflictions that obstruct renunciation;
the afflictions that obstruct receiving the noble status of humans and devas;
and the afflictions that obstruct the meditative concentration and meritorious bliss of birth in the form and formless realms.
Obstructing the attainment of sovereign supernormal powers, such as flying, ascending, becoming invisible, or manifesting,
and thus being unable to travel everywhere to the pure lands of the Buddhas of the ten directions.
The afflictions of listening to the Dharma obstruct the training in ānāpāna.
Counting the breaths; impurity;
causal conditions.
The afflictions such as views and so forth obstruct the stages of Heat and Peak in the training.
Patience,
the supreme dharma,
the seven stages of preparation, and so forth— these are all various afflictions.
It obstructs the cultivation of loving-kindness,
compassion, and sympathetic joy.
Abandoning the afflictions associated with hearing, reflection, and cultivation.
Obstructing the study of emptiness,
equality, and the understanding of the Middle Way.
The meaning of the three contemplations is that afflictions obstruct the factors conducive to enlightenment (bodhipakṣadharma) and the foundations of mindfulness (smṛtyupasthāna).
Right Effort,
the Faculties,
and the Powers.
The afflictions regarding the bases of psychic power obstruct the training in the Eightfold Noble Path;
these are the afflictions that manifest as signs.
The afflictions that do not manifest as signs obstruct the training in the seven factors of enlightenment; [the afflictions that manifest as signs] obstruct the training in the eight liberations.
The afflictions of the nine emptiness-concentrations obstruct the training in the ten knowledges and the three samādhis;
the afflictions obstruct the training in the three insights.
The six superknowledges (ṣaḍabhijñā) and the four unhindered [knowledges] (catasraḥ pratisaṃvidaḥ) are obstacles to the afflictions; they obstruct the training in the six perfections (ṣaṭpāramitā).
The four kinds of afflictions that obstruct the training in the four means of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*) are the afflictions that hinder extensive transformation [of sentient beings].
The afflictions that obstruct the aspiration for the Mahāyāna; the afflictions that obstruct the study of the four great vows;
and the afflictions that obstruct the study of the ten clarities and the ten practices.
The afflictions of the ten vows obstruct the study of the ten dedications;
they obstruct the study of the first stage.
The second stage,
the third stage,
and the fourth stage.
The affliction of conceptualizing through clear understanding obstructs training in the fifth and sixth stages.
The various knowledges, views, and afflictions of the seventh stage obstruct the training for the eighth and ninth stages.
The afflictions that simultaneously manifest on the ten stages, and so forth,
even obstructing the attainment of the Buddha-fruit.
The afflictions of a hundred thousand *asaṃkhyeya* formations are thus immeasurable and boundless. I,
the disciple [Name], today offer my most earnest prayers with deep prostration.
Before the Buddhas of the ten directions, the Honored Dharma, and the Noble Assembly, I confess with shame and remorse; may all [obstructions] be extinguished.
May I rely on this confession to bring all conditioned formations to an end.
May all the merits arising from the afflictions enable me to take birth with mastery wherever I may be,
and not be turned back by the accumulation of karmic actions.
By means of the supernormal power of psychic travel (*ṛddhividhi*), they reach all ten directions in a single thought-moment;
they purify all Buddha-fields and gather and transform sentient beings.
They penetrate without obstruction the profound realms of meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) as well as all forms of knowledge and vision (*jñānadarśana*).
The mind can universally pervade all phenomena with inexhaustible eloquence, yet remains unstained by attachment;
it attains mastery over the mind,
mastery over phenomena, and mastery over skillful means.
May these afflictions and the habitual tendencies of ignorance be utterly and permanently severed,
so that they no longer continue;
may the untainted noble path shine forth clearly like the sun.

Having made this vow, one takes refuge and pays homage to all Buddhas: Namo Vairocana Buddha. Namo Śākyamuni Buddha, our Original Teacher. Namo Amitābha Buddha. Namo Maitreya Buddha. Namo Nāgottamarāja Buddha. Namo Nāgeśvararāja Buddha. Namo Ratnasaṃbhava Buddha. Namo Bodhimaṇḍitavaiśvānararāja Buddha. Namo Kāṣāyadhvaja Buddha. Namo Siṃhanāda Buddha. Namo Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva. Namo Samantabhadra Bodhisattva. Namo Mahāsthāmaprāpta Bodhisattva. Namo Kṣitigarbha Bodhisattva. Namo Mahāvyūha Bodhisattva. Namo Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva. Having paid homage to all the Buddhas, [one continues].
Next, we shall again perform repentance.
We, [Name] and others, have briefly finished repenting for the obstacle of afflictions;
we shall now proceed in order to repent for the obstacle of karma.
Now, as for "karma," it is that which adorns the various realms of existence; wherever one may be, one no longer contemplates seeking liberation from the world.
This is why the retributions of the six paths of existence are diverse and their forms and types differ from one another.
One should know that all these are produced by the power of karma.
Among the ten powers of a Buddha, the power of karma is most profound.
Ordinary persons frequently give rise to doubts and delusions regarding this matter.
Why is this so? We observe in the world that those who practice virtue encounter misfortune at every turn,
while those who commit evil find their affairs prospering.
To say that there is no distinction between good and evil in the world—
those who hold such a view are all unable to penetrate deeply into the principles of karma. Why is this so?
The Sūtra states:
"There are three kinds of karma.
What are these three?"
First is retribution in the present life;
second is retribution in the next life;
third is retribution in subsequent lives.
Karma with immediate retribution refers to performing evil deeds in the present life and receiving the retribution in that same body.
Karma with retribution upon rebirth refers to...
"Wholesome or unwholesome deeds performed in this life result in retribution received in a future life.
As for karma that ripens in subsequent lives,
it refers to wholesome or unwholesome deeds performed during immeasurable past lives."
One may experience the retribution for this in the present life,
or one may experience its fruit only after immeasurable future lives. Thus,
it may happen that a person who currently practices evil appears to be flourishing in the present.
This is because the karmic fruits of past lives—both immediate and subsequent ripenings of wholesome karma—are now maturing;
it is for this reason that there is this fruit of happiness in the present.
How could it possibly be related to performing various evil deeds in the present to receive a favorable retribution?
If those who currently practice virtue are now beset by suffering,
this is because the retributive karma of past lives— whether as immediate retribution or subsequent retribution— is ripening;
thus, the power of their present roots of goodness is too weak to dispel it.
Therefore, one receives this retribution of suffering.
How could this possibly be related to performing good deeds in the present that result in an evil retribution?
How is this known to be so?
We observe in the world that those who perform wholesome deeds are praised by others and respected by others; therefore,
we know that they will certainly bring about pleasant fruits in the future.
Since such evil karma exists from the past,
the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas have taught that one should draw near to virtuous friends and together perform repentance.
A virtuous friend is of complete benefit in the attainment of the Way.
For this reason, today we take refuge in the Buddha with utmost sincerity.
From time immemorial until this day, [we, such-and-such persons...]
Accumulating evil like the sands of the Ganges and committing sins that fill the great earth,
one casts off this body and receives another,
neither perceiving nor knowing it.
Some commit the grave karma of the five heinous crimes, bound by dense and turbid afflictions;
some create the karma of an icchantika who severs the roots of goodness;
and some commit the karma of slandering the Mahāyāna sūtras by lightly misrepresenting the Buddha’s words.
The karma of destroying the Triple Gem and subverting the True Dharma;
the karma of disbelieving in sin and merit while giving rise to the ten unwholesome actions;
and the karma of delusion and confusion that mistakes the false for the true.
The karma of being unfilial toward one's two parents and acting with perverse contrariness;
the karma of treating teachers and elders with contempt and lacking in ritual respect;
and the karma of being untrustworthy toward friends and devoid of righteousness.
Or they may create karma that constitutes fourfold or eightfold obstructions to the Noble Path;
karma that violates the five precepts or breaks the eight fast-day observances;
or karma that involves numerous omissions and transgressions of the five categories and seven groups of offenses.
The upāsaka precepts involve heavy or light defiled karma;
or the bodhisattva precepts may fail to be pure according to the prescribed practices;
or the preliminary and subsequent applications may defile the practice of the Brahma-conduct.
There is no practice of the six monthly fasts (*ṣaḍ-upoṣadha*) and the karma of indolence;
the three long fasts (*tri-dīrgha-upoṣadha*) are not constantly cultivated;
and the three thousand dignified conducts (*trīṇi sahasrāṇi īryāpathāni*) do not accord with the Dharma.
The eighty thousand subtle offenses of the disciplinary code (*vinaya*),
the failure to cultivate the karma of body, precepts, mind, and wisdom,
and the various sinful karmas created during the eight kings of spring and autumn.
They practice sixteen kinds of unwholesome, non-restraint-based actions;
they possess no karma of compassion toward sentient beings,
no karma of regard or mindfulness, and no karma of pity.
The karma of neither uprooting nor rescuing, which provides no protection;
the karma of harboring envy, which lacks the means to deliver others;
and the karma of partiality toward the spheres of enemies and kin.
They indulge in the five desires without weariness or renunciation;
or, due to clothing, food, gardens, groves, ponds, or pools, they give rise to dissolute and negligent karma;
or, in the prime of their youth, they abandon themselves to lustful passions and commit a multitude of sinful karmas.
Or having performed tainted wholesome deeds that dedicate [merit] toward the three realms of existence, thereby obstructing supramundane karma—
such immeasurable and boundless transgressions as these,
I today disclose before the Buddhas of the ten directions, the Honored Dharma, and the Noble Assembly.
I repent of them all.
May [Name] and others, by virtue of this repentance,
be freed from the offenses of ignorance and the like.
May all unwholesome karmas be completely extinguished.
May the merit and goodness thus generated ensure that in every life and every age, the five heinous crimes are eradicated and the delusions of icchantikas are eliminated.
From this day forward, until I reach the site of enlightenment, I vow never again to commit any such light or heavy sinful karmas;
I shall constantly practice the pure, wholesome dharmas that transcend the world.
He maintained the disciplinary practices with precision and guarded his dignified demeanor,
like one crossing the sea who cherishes a life-preserving float.
The six perfections and four immeasurable minds were always held as the foremost of his conduct.
The categories of morality, concentration, and wisdom will become increasingly bright and clear.
One will swiftly accomplish the thirty-two marks and eighty minor characteristics of a Tathāgata,
as well as the ten powers, the fearlessnesses, great compassion, the three constant mindfulnesses, wondrous wisdom, and the eightfold self-mastery.
We take refuge in all Buddhas; may you deign to protect and sustain us with your compassionate mindfulness.
We, [Name] and others, have previously performed a general confession of all our karmic actions.
Now, I shall proceed in order to further perform the confession of each individual characteristic separately—
whether in general or in detail, whether coarse or subtle,
whether light or heavy, and whether confessed or unconfessed.
May all [faults] categorized by their respective characteristics be extinguished through these vows.
Regarding the confession of specific characteristics:
first, one confesses the three [misdeeds] of the body.
Next, one repents the four [misdeeds] of speech.
For the remaining obstacles, one prostrates in succession.
Regarding the three karmas of the body:
First is killing.
As clarified in the sutras,
one may take oneself as an analogy for this.
Do not kill; do not wield the staff.
Although there are differences between humans and beasts, the preservation of life and the fear of death are one and the same for all.
If one investigates these sentient beings,
from beginningless time they have been one's own parents, brothers, or members of the six classes of relatives;
yet, due to the causes and conditions of karma, they have transmigrated through the six realms of existence.
Passing from birth into death, they undergo transformations and receive retributions such that they no longer recognize one another;
yet now you give rise to malice and devour their flesh—
this is the height of injury to compassion.
Therefore, the Buddha said:
"Even if you obtain extra food, you should regard it as if in a time of famine,
with the thought that it is the flesh of your own son."
How much less, then, should one eat the flesh of these fish?
It is further said:
"For the sake of profit, they kill sentient beings and use wealth as a net to obtain various meats."
Both are evil karmas;
at death, one falls into the Raurava Hell.
Thus, it is known that both killing and devouring [are likewise].
The depth of our transgressions exceeds that of rivers and seas, and their gravity surpasses that of hills and mountains.
Yet, from time immemorial, we, such-and-such individuals, have failed to encounter virtuous friends, and all this is due to these very karmic actions.
Therefore, a sutra says:
The sin of killing causes sentient beings to fall into the hells or as hungry ghosts to undergo suffering;
if they are born among animals, they receive the bodies of tigers, leopards, jackals, wolves, hawks, or falcons.
Some receive the bodies of venomous snakes, vipers, scorpions, and the like,
constantly harboring evil intentions;
others receive the bodies of deer, roe deer, bears, brown bears, and so forth.
They constantly harbor fear.
If they are born among humans, they will receive two kinds of retribution:
first, they will suffer from many illnesses.
Second is a short lifespan.
Since there are such immeasurable and various evil retributions resulting from killing and devouring,
one should therefore seek refuge with utmost sincerity and repent.
We, such-and-such persons, from time immemorial until this day,
have possessed this mind-consciousness that has constantly harbored cruelty and malice, lacking any heart of compassion.
We have, at times, committed killing out of greed.
One kills out of anger, out of delusion, or out of pride;
or one employs evil means, vowing to kill, wishing to kill,
or killing through incantations.
Or they breach and drain lakes and ponds;
they set fire to mountains and wilds;
and they hunt, fish, and trap.
Or they may set fires by fanning them with wind,
or release hawks and dogs to harass and harm all living beings.
I now repent of all such offenses as these:
whether by means of cages, snares, pits, traps, spears, halberds, bows,
or crossbows, shooting at birds and beasts of the wild.
Or they use nets, snares, and hooks to scoop up and filter aquatic creatures such as fish, turtles, soft-shelled turtles, crocodiles, shrimp, clams, and snails— all those that dwell in moisture—
leaving them with no place to hide or flee among the water, land, or air.
Some raise chickens, pigs, cattle, sheep, dogs, swine, geese, ducks,
and the like for their own use in the kitchen;
others sell them to others for slaughter.
Causing their plaintive cries to end only as their feathers and fur fall out, their scales and shells are mangled and destroyed, and their bodies and heads are severed;
their flesh and bones are wasted away and crushed, flayed and torn apart, butchered and sliced, roasted, burned, boiled, and grilled, undergoing agonizing and piercing suffering.
To inflict harm upon the innocent is merely to seek momentary gratification; the flavor gained for the mouth is exceedingly meager,
lasting no longer than the span of a three-inch tongue.
Yet the retribution for these offenses will entail calamities and karmic burdens for eternal kalpas.
All such sins as these, we now sincerely repent of them all.
Furthermore, from time immemorial until this very day—
Or they may raise armies to attack one another, with borders in conflict;
the two opposing forces face each other, killing and slaying one another.
Or they may kill themselves, incite others to kill, or take joy upon hearing of killing.
Some practice the slaughter of animals or hire themselves out for execution,
cooking and slaughtering the lives of others in acts of cruelty;
others indulge their violent rage, brandishing halberds and brandishing blades.
Some were beheaded, some were stabbed;
some were pushed into pits and ditches,
while others were drowned in water.
Some block their burrows and destroy their nests;
some pelt them with earth and stones;
others, with the thundering rattle of chariots and horses, trample all sentient beings underfoot.
Such offenses as these are immeasurable and boundless;
today we reveal them all and repent of them entirely.
Furthermore, from time immemorial until this very day:
Or they cause abortions and destroy embryos;
they harm and kill sentient beings through poisons and sorcery;
they plow the soil and dig the earth to plant fields and orchards, and they raise silkworms and boil cocoons.
Injuries and killings were exceedingly frequent.
Some struck and killed mosquitoes and gnats, or pinched and bit fleas and lice;
others burned away refuse or dug out ditches and channels.
They wrongfully harm all living beings;
some devour fruits and seeds,
while others consume grains and rice.
Or they may kill living beings by cutting through vegetables and herbs;
or they may burn firewood.
Or one may expose lamps and candles, thereby burning various insects;
or one may take up sauces or vinegar without first stirring them;
or one may pour out hot water, thereby killing insects and ants.
In this way, even throughout the four modes of conduct— walking, standing, sitting, and lying down—
they constantly injure and kill minute sentient beings, whether flying through the air or dwelling upon the ground;
yet ordinary people, their consciousness being shrouded in darkness, neither perceive nor know this.
Today we disclose and repent of them all.
Furthermore, from time immemorial until this day, we have used whips, staves, shackles, fetters, and manacles;
we have subjected others to crushing, pulling, torturing, beating, and hurling.
They torment sentient beings through various evil means, such as kicking and trampling with their hands and feet, binding and confining them in cages, and depriving them of water and food.
Today, with utmost sincerity, I confess before the Buddhas of the ten directions, the Honored Dharma,
and the Assembly of Sages. I pray that by virtue of this confession, may [all merits] be received.
Regarding such sins as killing and the like,
the merit thereby produced will cause one to attain a vajra-body in every successive birth;
one’s lifespan shall be infinite, one will forever be free from enmity and hatred, and one will harbor no thought of killing.
Regarding all sentient beings, they attain the stage of regarding them as an only son.
If they see those in peril, danger, or urgent distress,
they do not begrudge their own bodies or lives, employing skillful means to rescue and liberate them.
Thereafter, he shall preach the subtle and sublime True Dharma,
so that all sentient beings who behold his form or see his shadow shall receive peace and happiness,
and those who hear his name or listen to his voice shall have all their fears entirely dispelled.

I now prostrate my forehead to the ground and take refuge in the Buddha. Homage to Vairocana Buddha; homage to our Original Teacher Śākyamuni Buddha; homage to Amitābha Buddha; homage to Maitreya Buddha; homage to Nāgottamarāja Buddha; homage to Nāgeśvararāja Buddha; homage to Ratnasaṃbhava Buddha; homage to Bodhimaṇḍeśvararāja Buddha; homage to Kāṣāyadhvaja Buddha; homage to Siṃhanāda Buddha; homage to Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva; homage to Samantabhadra Bodhisattva; homage to Mahāsthāmaprāpta Bodhisattva; homage to Kṣitigarbha Bodhisattva; homage to Mahāvyūha Bodhisattva; homage to Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva. Having paid homage to all the Buddhas, [I take refuge].
Next, we again perform repentance.
We, [Name] and others, next repent of the karma of robbery and theft.
As it is said in the sutras:
If an object belongs to another and is guarded by another,
one does not take even a single blade of grass or a single leaf from among those objects without it being given.
How much more so for theft?
It is simply because sentient beings perceive only immediate benefits that they take by various unrighteous means.
This causes one to suffer such calamities and consequences in the future.
Therefore, the Sūtra says:
"The sin of stealing can cause sentient beings to fall into the hells or the realm of hungry ghosts to undergo suffering."
If one is born among animals, one assumes the form of an ox, horse, donkey, mule, camel, or the like,
repaying past debts with the physical strength, flesh, and blood of that body. If one is born among humans,
one becomes a slave or servant for others.
Their clothing does not cover their bodies and their food does not fill their mouths;
impoverished, cold, and suffering, their humanity is nearly extinguished.
Since such bitter retributions exist for those who commit robbery and theft, [one must refrain from them].
Therefore, today we most sincerely seek compassion and repent.
From time immemorial until this day, we, [Name] and others,
have perhaps stolen the wealth and treasures of others, or used blades to seize them by force.
Some take them by exerting themselves physically to coerce them;
some rely on public authority;
and some resort to power and influence, employing high gallows and heavy shackles.
They oppress the virtuous and swallow illicit bribes;
they pervert the upright into the crooked.
For these reasons, they fall into the net of the law.
Or they may govern with perverse methods, seizing the property of others;
encroaching upon public interests for private gain or private interests for public gain;
harming others to benefit oneself or harming oneself to benefit others.
They exploit others for their own profit while harboring stinginess in speech and heart;
they may even embezzle taxes and assessments or steal across passes and ferries.
I repent of all such offenses as concealing public taxes and hiding corvée laborers.
Furthermore, from time immemorial until this day:
Or taking what belongs to the Buddha, Dharma, or Sangha without it being given;
or objects belonging to scriptures or images;
or objects used for the maintenance of stupas or monasteries.
Whether it be property belonging to the permanently resident Sangha,
or property intended for the Sangha of the four quarters,
they may steal it, misappropriate it, or, relying on their power, refuse to return it.
Either one borrows for oneself, or lends to others,
or again, through exchange or lending, there is forgetfulness.
Or they may have confused and indiscriminately used the property of the Triple Gem;

or they may have used the communal property— such as grain, rice, firewood, salt, fermented soybeans, sauces, vinegar, vegetables, fruits, money, silk, bamboo, wood, brocades, banners, canopies, incense, flowers, oil, and candles.
Following one's feelings and inclinations,
one may either use it oneself or give it to others.
Or they pluck the flowers and fruits of the Buddha for their own use, or misappropriate the property of the Sangha;
by privately benefiting themselves with the wealth and goods belonging to the Triple Gem,
they commit such immeasurable and boundless transgressions as these.
Today, with a sense of shame and remorse, I confess all of these. Furthermore,
from time immemorial until this day, whether acting as a companion or otherwise,
I have committed various transgressions.
Friends, preceptors, fellow students, parents, brothers, and the six classes of kinsmen live and dwell together;
regarding the hundred and one necessities of life, they deceive and defraud one another,
or do so among neighbors and those living nearby.
They move fences and expand walls to encroach upon the lands and residences of others;
they alter boundary markers and change landmarks to plunder wealth and property;
and they seize and occupy fields and gardens under the pretext of public business while pursuing private interests.
I now repent of all such sins as seizing others' shops, residences, and estates in the fields and wilderness.
Furthermore, from time immemorial, [I have committed these offenses].
They may assault cities, destroy towns, burn villages, and demolish stockades;
they may steal and sell free commoners or entice away the servants of others;
or they may further unjustly oppress those who are innocent.
It causes their bodies to perish by the edge of a sword while their kin remain bound in chains;
family ties are shattered and flesh-and-blood are separated;
they are dispersed to different realms, with life and death forever severed.
I now repent of all such immeasurable and boundless transgressions.
Furthermore, from time immemorial until this day, whether in commerce, trade,
or the management of shops and markets, [I have committed various offenses].
Using light scales and small measures, they reduce dimensions;
they steal fractions of a grain and deceive others with slight variations in volume;
they exchange coarse goods for the fine and short items for the long.
I now repent of all such offenses as these— employing a hundred forms of deceitful guile in the hope of gaining even a hair’s breadth of profit.
Furthermore, from beginningless time until this very day, [I have committed such transgressions].
Breaking through walls and climbing over fences, cutting off roads to plunder;
evading debts and interest;
being ungrateful and violating agreements; and taking by deceiving others face-to-face.

How is this known to be so?
Śakra Devānām Indra beheld the five signs of decay;

"None of you should rely upon your youth, wealth, power, or influence to become indolent, lazy, heedless, or self-indulgent.

It arrives suddenly without anyone’s knowledge.
Human life is impermanent, comparable to morning dew;

Why do you suddenly neglect this and fail to repent?

In the prime of life and the vigor of youth, none can escape this fate.

Wife, children, and kinsmen are no longer my kin;

Speaking from this perspective:
The retributions of the world are all illusory transformations.

Compared to this, the manifold sufferings of hell are [infinitely greater].
